# Implement block: Sticker Board (Jetpack Compose)

You are adding the "Sticker Board" block from Native Cook to the user's Android app. The block already exists as working Kotlin code. Your job is to bring it into this project faithfully, not to write a new one that looks similar.

## The block

A cork board covered in die-cut stickers with thick white borders and soft shadows: round and rounded photo stickers of fruit and dogs, a star, a smiley, a pink speech bubble, a green scalloped seal and a heart, under a strip of masking tape with the board's name. Any sticker can be dragged, turned with two fingers and pinched at the same time; it lifts as it is picked up and slaps down with a squash when let go. A long press lifts a corner instead: it curls back over the sticker after the finger, showing its pale backing, until the sticker comes off. Then a small steel pedal bin rises from the bottom edge, leans towards the loose sticker and opens its hinged lid as it comes near, pulls it in over its mouth, and on release crumples it into a paper ball that drops in before the lid slams shut and the number on the bin ticks up.

**Motion.** Everything is drawn on one canvas over a cork shader (on Android below 13, a plain warm ground with the same vignette); the bin is vector drawing with no blur on it, only on its contact shadow. A picked-up sticker comes to the top without jumping over the stickers that covered it: a copy stays in its old place in the pile while the one on top fades in over 0.26 s (ease-in-out), so it surfaces through them as it lifts; it grows 6% and its shadow moves from 1×2 pt (blur 2.2) to 6×16 pt (blur 11) with a 0.12 s time constant, and it swings up to 10° with its speed (0.012° per pt/s). Dragging follows the finger with a 40 pt rubber band at the screen's edges; a release keeps the finger's speed (capped at 1500 pt/s) gliding with a 0.09 s time constant while it falls over 0.16 s, aimed to land on the board, then slaps down with a squash (8.5% wider and flatter) that springs out with one soft rebound (stiffness 480, damping 19) with a medium haptic. Two fingers turn it freely and scale it between 0.55 and 2.2, rubber-banded beyond. Holding 420 ms lifts the corner nearest the finger (light haptic): the fold is the line halfway between that corner and the finger, the part beyond it is mirrored across it as the backing, bright along the crease and greyer to the tip, casting a soft shadow on the rest. Pulled further than 1.25 times the corner's distance from the middle, the sticker comes off (rigid haptic), the flap lies flat over 0.22 s and the sticker follows the finger lifted 1.4 times as high; let go before that, the flap lies back down. While a corner is up the bin rises from below the screen on a spring (stiffness 300, damping 21) to stand 18 pt above the bottom safe area. A loose sticker within 300 pt of the point 72 pt over the bin's mouth makes the bin lean towards it (up to 9°), grow up to 7% and open its lid in proportion (up to 85% of 100° on a spring of stiffness 240, damping 15, so it overshoots a little); within 92 pt (sticker or finger) the bin takes it: the lid opens fully, the sticker is pulled 82% of the way to the mouth and shrinks by 30% on a spring (stiffness 360, damping 19), with a selection haptic. Let go there, or flicked towards the bin faster than 800 pt/s from within 460 pt, the sticker crumples over 0.34 s into a lumpy 16 pt paper ball (its outline morphs point by point, its picture shrinks inside, facets and creases fade in, 170° of spin) while it moves over the mouth, then drops in on a 16 pt hop over 0.3 s; the lid slams (stiffness 1500, damping 14) and bounces off the rim at 32% of its speed, the bin squashes and wobbles on springs, the counter's digits roll up over 0.34 s, and a success haptic fires on the slam frame. Let go anywhere else, it drops on the board. The bin tucks away 0.9 s after the slam. A sticker thrown away is slapped back in its place 4 s later; the counter wraps at 100. autoPlay plays a 15 s LOOP from rest: the cherries are carried on an arc, turned 18° and dropped (0.6–2.2 s), the dog card turned −26° and scaled to 1.28 (3.0–4.6 s), the lemons, which the dog card has landed on, pressed at 5.0 s and rising through it onto the top of the pile, then peeled from the corner (5.45–6.9 s), carried towards the bin (6.9–8.0 s) where the magnet takes them, let go at 8.5 s to crumple, drop in and slam at about 9.15 s, the first two carried home (9.7–11.1, 11.4–12.8 s) and the lemons slapped back on at about 12.5 s; the counter starts each loop at 0. A touch pauses it; 3.5 s after the last touch every sticker glides home over 0.9 s and the loop starts again. Under reduced motion the loop does not play, there is no grow, glide, squash, lean, wobble or crumple: the bin fades in and out, its lid opens without a spring, and a thrown sticker fades out where it was let go.

## Reference source

The block is built and running in the Native Cook source repository. Each link below is a file on GitHub. To read one as plain text, replace `https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/` with `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/` in its address.

## Your instructions

_Anything specific to this app goes here: where the block should appear, what to rename, what to change. Left empty, integrate the block as it is._

## How to work

Work like an experienced Android engineer joining an existing project: learn the app first, read only what you need, decide early how the block fits, then integrate it with as little disruption as possible. Take the steps in order.

**Done means** the block is reachable in the user's app and behaves like the reference on an emulator or a device. A Compose preview is useful while you work, but it is not the proof: build, install and run the app.

**Fidelity.** Bring over the real implementation. Keep its structure, colours, sizes, timings and easing. Change only what this project requires and what "Your instructions" ask for.

If you already learned this project earlier in the conversation, reuse what you know and skip step 2. Learn it again only if the project changed or something you need is missing.

### 1. Check where you are

- You need the project's files and a terminal. If this prompt was pasted into a chat that has neither, stop and say so: it has to be run by a coding agent opened on the project.
- Confirm the project is an Android app built with Gradle. If it is something else, stop, say what you found, and do not create a new app inside it unless the instructions ask for one.

### 2. Learn the host app

- The app module, its namespace, `minSdk`, `compileSdk`, and the versions of Kotlin, the Android Gradle Plugin and Compose (a BOM or single versions).
- Whether Compose is switched on in that module, and whether screens are Compose, Views or both.
- Navigation: Navigation Compose, fragments, activities, or a single screen. Find how a screen is added today.
- How dependencies are declared: a version catalog (`libs.versions.toml`) or directly in `build.gradle`.
- Conventions: package layout, naming, theme, where resources live and how they are named.

### 3. Read the block

- Open the demo, then each file in the block's package. The list above names every file of the block, and the resources it uses from outside its package.
- The demo is how the source repository shows the block. Bring over what the demo shows, not the repository's gallery. Anything listed under "Used by the demo only" stays behind.
- Read the block's parameters and their defaults. The demo may switch on an option that makes the block play by itself for a recording (for example `autoPlay`). Keep the option; leave it off in the user's app unless asked.

### 4. Decide the fit

- Compare the block's libraries and the versions it was built with to the host's. Add what is missing the way this project declares dependencies. Do not upgrade the host's Kotlin, Gradle plugin or Compose versions without asking; if an API differs on the host's version, adapt the block's code.
- Check `minSdk`. If the block uses an API newer than the host's minimum, keep the fallback the source has, or tell the user what would be lost.
- If Compose is not switched on in the module, say what turning it on involves before you do it. In a View-based screen, show the block through a `ComposeView`.
- Shared helpers: copy the ones the block imports next to it, or fold them into the block's files. Do not copy helpers it never calls.

### 5. Bring it in

- Copy the block's files into a package of this app, and rewrite the `package` lines and the imports, including the import of the app's own `R` class.
- Copy its resources and asset files. Keep their names unless one collides with a resource of the app; then rename it everywhere it is used.
- Keep reduced-motion handling, haptics and accessibility descriptions as they are in the source. If the block needs a permission, add it to the manifest and say so.
- Mount the block where the instructions say. With no instructions, add a screen or destination named after the block and make it reachable the way the app's other screens are.

### 6. Run it

- Build with the project's own task, for example `./gradlew :app:assembleDebug`, and fix every error and new warning the block introduced.
- Install and run it, and use the block: every state, every gesture, and once with animations switched off in the system settings.
- If the build or the emulator fails for a reason outside the block, report the error and ask how to continue.

### 7. Report

- Files added and changed, dependencies and permissions added, and anything renamed to avoid a collision.
- How to reach the block in the app.
- Anything that differs from the reference, and why.
